column11: And therefore the Sages taught (Berakhot 18b): the wicked in their lifetimes are called dead, for genuine life issues from the soul; but if one cleaves to corporeal lusts of the body, his soul-faculties remain mere shadows, and he is termed dead, just as upon the departure of his soul he is physically dead. But one who cleaves to Hashem God of Truth—which our Sages expounded (Jerusalem Talmud, Sanhedrin 1:1; Bereishit Rabbah 81:2; Vayikra Rabbah 26:1): why is He called Truth? Because He is the living God and eternal King.

column9: Shabbat 24a: ‘A dilemma was raised before the Sages: What is the ruling with regard to the obligation to mention Hanukkah in Grace after Meals? The dilemma is: Since it is merely an obligation by rabbinic law, do we not mention it? Or, perhaps due to publicity of the miracle, we mention it. Rava said that Rav Seḥora said that Rav Huna said: One does not mention it. And if, nevertheless, he comes to mention it, he mentions it in the blessing of thanksgiving. The Gemara relates that Rav Huna bar Yehuda happened by Rava’s house on Hanukkah. When, after eating, he came to recite Grace after Meals, he thought to mention Hanukkah in the blessing: Who builds Jerusalem. Rav Sheshet said to the yeshiva…’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 15 — Rosh Chodesh Tevet and the Sixth Day of Chanukah, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 24a) to illuminate his statement here (“just as the dilemma was raised in the Gemara (Shabbat 24a): "What is the law regarding mentioning Chanukah in the Musaf prayers?", which refers to both Shabbat and Rosh Chodesh that occur during Chanukah; and as he...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.
column11: And cosmic creation as a whole is circular or spherical, endowed with kinetic movement, just as the soul and mental thoughts never quiet nor rest, except at death, which is termed by our Sages in their elegant phrasing: "his soul came to rest" (nach nafshei), having acquired the faculty of rest. column13: As in Yalkut Shimoni (Samuel 124): When Samuel saw David was ruddy, he thought: “Perhaps he is a murderer like Esau?” until the Holy One showed him that David operated solely through justice. From this we see that the early generations lacked discernment to separate good from evil; for though made upright, they had to draw bodily sustenance from nature which contained good and evil; and instinct without discernment branches into evil—just as unguided compassion can cruelly pity the wicked.

And the word “Bereishit” alludes to challah, terumah, etc., teaching that man must return the primary inception of all bounty back to the Blessed Name; and within that initial dedication the entire expansion of creation is bound up, so that he realizes through it that every dynamic force originates solely from Him.

column9: Bereshit Rabbah 11: ‘“God blessed the seventh day [and sanctified it]” – Rabbi Yishmael said: He blessed it with manna and He sanctified it with manna. He blessed it with manna in that all the days of the week one omer [of manna] would fall, while on the day before Shabbat two omers would fall. for Shabbat. He sanctified it with manna, as it did not fall on it [on Shabbat] at all. Rabbi Natan says: He blessed it with manna and sanctified it with a blessing. Rabbi Yitzḥak said: He blessed it with manna and sanctified it through the gatherer. He blessed it with apparel. Rav Huna said: He should change his clothing. Rabbi Ḥiyya said in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan: He should mix [garments]. Avin bar Ḥisdai said:…’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 15 — Rosh Chodesh Tevet and the Sixth Day of Chanukah, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Bereshit Rabbah 11) to illuminate his statement here (“And chanu means rest, as they expounded chanayah as an expression of rest (Bereishit Rabbah, Parashah 11) regarding Jacob of whom Sabbath observance is written: "And he encamped (vayichan), etc.", – for the workdays...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.

column11: And the Sages taught (Bereishit Rabbah 11:8) that the Sabbath complained: "Every day has a partner, but I have no partner!", to which Hashem replied: "The Congregation of Israel shall be your partner." The explanation: every created composite necessarily harbors a bestowing impulse through which it yearns to channel influence. And since the Sabbath is cessation and the cessation of physical labor, it seemingly possessed no recipient to bestow upon, complaining: "Every day has a partner"—an operative vessel of reception—"while I have no partner".

column9: Pesachim 50a: ‘Rabbi Aḥa bar Ḥanina said: The World-to-Come is not like this world. In this world, upon good tidings one recites: Blessed…Who is good and does good, and over bad tidings one recites: Blessed…the true Judge. In the World-to-Come one will always recite: Blessed…Who is good and does good. There will be only one mode of blessing God for tidings.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 15 — Rosh Chodesh Tevet and the Sixth Day of Chanukah, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Pesachim 50a) to illuminate his statement here (“And this is based on what is stated in the Gemara (Pesachim 50a): – "'On that day Hashem shall be One' — is He then not One today, etc.? In the World to Come it will be entirely the blessing of 'He Who is good and...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.

column9: Yoma 69a: ‘The Gemara considers resolving the dilemma from the latter clause: They remove their priestly vestments and fold them and place them under their heads. The Gemara suggests: Learn from this that it is permitted to derive benefit from priestly vestments. Rav Pappa said: Do not say that the mishna means they may actually place the vestments under their heads as a pillow; rather, say that the mishna permits the vestments to be placed only next to their heads. Rav Mesharshiyya said: Given this understanding of that mishna, one can learn from here that one who places phylacteries to the side of his head when he sleeps has done well; there is no concern that he will turn over in his sleep and…’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 15 — Rosh Chodesh Tevet and the Sixth Day of Chanukah, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Yoma 69a) to illuminate his statement here (“whereas previously they had been subjugated to them, forcing Shimon the Righteous to go out to meet Alexander (Yoma 69a), and had it not been for the decrees, they certainly would not have arisen against him; only...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.
